Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season.
  • Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'massive six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
  • Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season.

Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'massive six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.

Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?

While Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.

But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.

United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.

But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.

While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.

Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

Sources indicate that but what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement rapidly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are at the moment taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.

By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.

While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.

History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.

Recent findings suggest that of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.

In a recent development, A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.

Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.

Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.

It is a substantial ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.

Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last term.

Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.

While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams at the moment in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals.

So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his newly introduced club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

Inside the mind games that will decide Arsenal v Man City

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • Industry observers note that manchester City have a lot of bigger concerns right now but some of Enzo Maresca’s staff have naturally been conscious of the noise around David Raya.
  • It’s certainly true the injury suffered at Newcastle United is nowhere near as bad as first feared, with contact on a nerve having apparently caused the initial concern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Industry observers note that manchester City have a lot of bigger concerns right now but some of Enzo Maresca’s staff have naturally been conscious of the noise around David Raya. The goalkeeper was not wearing a sling at Tuesday’s Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund, after he had so conspicuously been photographed sporting one on London’s busiest street just two days before.

It’s certainly true the injury suffered at Newcastle United is nowhere near as bad as first feared, with contact on a nerve having apparently caused the initial concern.

Some on the City side have wondered whether Mikel Arteta is using it to play his usual games. The manager likes to use media and even official squad photos to keep opposition guessing.

It would be especially understandable here, since this position could go a long way to deciding Sunday’s game.

The entire decision on Raya, in fact, draws out so many of its strands and storylines.

Both sides are especially attuned to it since it was as recently as March's Carabao Cup final that Pep Guardiola’s response to the Kepa Arrizabalaga selection essentially decided that game.

According to recent reports, it might even have been the Catalan’s last piece of genius in England. Arsenal couldn’t play out of the press without Raya's passing, and City gradually shut them down. The tactical effect of it was so pronounced that it framed the thinking of both clubs ahead of April’s suffocatingly tense Premier League showdown.

That 2-1 City win might well go down as one of those influential defeats, rather than decisive victories, because of the effect on Arsenal. They actually gleaned confidence and instruction, to win all of their remaining games.

And now they're champions, and intent on asserting exactly what that means - with Raya's injury presently the primary concern.

Except, aside from it looking 50-50 over whether Raya will be involved, Guardiola certainly won’t be. The man responsible for that tactical thinking isn't there. And even if there is now debate over Maresca’s exact quality as a coach, he’s not Guardiola.

The dysfunction of his own pressing system, and City’s newly profound susceptibility to counter-attacks, also means they may not be able to execute any such approach in the same way… but then very little about City is the same.

The very consequence of this match might even change.

It all adds to the feel of this being a defining game for this most peculiar of seasons.

Recent findings suggest that arsenal can win to emphatically kill City’s title challenge… but will that even be a title challenge? City can win to transform the entire dynamic around the top of the table, but will the outcome of their appeal skew it in a way the Premier League has never seen?

Or, what if they win and then win their appeal - however unlikely legal figures right now think that is - to then go on a run?

It’s an absurd context, and that for a fixture that has recently been freighted with greater meaning.

And it is because of that recent history that Arsenal do feel they owe City one.

Arteta is said to feel it was absolutely crucial they won the title before Guardiola left and the verdict of the long-running Premier League case came in.

It was about proving it on their own terms. And now, with City precarious, they want to fully prove their superiority; to emphasise this can be their era; to put City out of the picture.

Despite enduring two comebacks for draws in their last two matches, the Arsenal squad are in a good mood.

They feel they played excellently for 160 minutes of those games and that just continuing that will have them in good stead over an awkward run of fixtures.

Or, as one figure told the Independent: “We are due to hammer someone”.

And, as another said separately: “We need to hammer City on Sunday”.

Everyone at Arsenal knows that is much easier said than done.

Despite all of City’s recent problems, the rivalry of this fixture might just be the type of game Maresca’s side require. It might cause them to dig deep.

That of course may depend on how deep their problems actually are.

One recent argument coming out of City has been that this is all just tactical, and individual moments in individual games are going against them.

It’s just that the idea this slump is solely down to tactical/technical problems feels… a stretch.

Really, City are in a situation of remarkable extremes.

In a recent development, even the departure of Guardiola would have been enough to distort an entire season. If City are obviously better structured than Manchester United after Sir Alex Ferguson or Arsenal themselves after Arsene Wenger, it is still adapting to the absence of one of the most psychologically imposing figures in football. His presence was immense.

That alone creates a vacuum, that is arguably manifesting in City's dysfunctional midfield.

In a recent development, that area also poses significant tactical questions about Guardiola's successor. Insiders familiar with both Chelsea and Leicester City can’t help notice familiar flaws in Maresca’s teams, especially as regards the balance. City are just so easy to get at.

Industry observers note that you can even map previous Chelsea form onto this season. Maresca’s first season at Stamford Bridge in 2024-25 started well, to the point of being talked of as title challengers, only to endure a winter drop-off surrounded by the same tactical discussions.

And then, there’s the guilty verdict.

In a recent development, the City squad are going through a situation no one in English football history has ever experienced. You can even extend that to European football, despite various controversies, given how long this entire process has been.

Another line from inside the club is that they are as adamant with the players as they are with everyone else: that they will overturn this verdict, and big questions will instead be posted to the rest of the Premier League.

Some at rival clubs even think that one element of City’s belligerent response, at least in public, has been as a message to the players.

It has been revealed that they need to radiate a sense of business as usual so as to convince the squad, because they do need the actual football business to indeed be as it usually is. They know they need to keep them focused.

That’s just very difficult to do when the potential consequences could come this season, which recent results arguably show.

Because, even if the players themselves honestly insist they are genuinely fully focused, this is still a story that has major implications for their careers. They may have to take substantial decisions. Some might even be thinking this is a waste of a season in a short career.

That is going to at least have some effect, even if it is subconscious.

It creates a cloud of doubt, and this in a sport that demands more intensity of focus than ever before. The opposition manager, Arteta, demands it more than anyone else. Guardiola himself was a huge influence in this.

Both have abruptly discarded numerous players if they sensed that a necessary tunnel vision had been obscured by even 1 per cent.

Recent findings suggest that and that is exactly what a situation like this does. It's too substantial to just completely shut out.

Without it, City might have even been better able to work around some of the tactical issues.

In short, even if performances have been OK, this does not look like a team playing to optimum level.

In a recent development, neither do Arsenal but they don’t feel too far off. They're primed. City might well need that challenge to rouse themselves.

Either way, it is already a fixture that feels like it has the makings of a huge result. And also a result that might mean absolutely nothing by the end.

One person had a worse night than United keeper – the wretched referee

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By the end of another utterly chaotic 90 minutes in the Manchester United soap opera, there was only one person who had endured a worse night than Senne Lammens.

Watching this game back will make for grim viewing for the United goalkeeper who, having been one of the club’s shining lights last season, is steadily becoming enveloped in a crisis of his own in this most torrid of campaigns.

But Roberto Rosetti, Uefa’s chief refereeing officer, might also want to sit Szymon Marciniak down after this and pick over the Polish official’s own nightmare performance. Marciniak denied United two goals, both of which should have stood, and in doing so ended up shining an even more brutal lens on Lammens’s calamitous display.

United’s Belgian goalkeeper was responsible for both of Sporting’s goals. He needlessly conceded a penalty in the first half, after a rush of blood to the head, that was converted by Luis Suárez, just 75 seconds after he had saved a spot-kick from the Sporting striker.

United had recovered from those bewildering few minutes to lead early in the second half, courtesy of two goals from captain Bruno Fernandes against his old club.

In a recent development, but, 10 minutes from time, Lammens committed the kind of howler that becomes worse and worse with every viewing. In doing so, he handed Sporting an equaliser and ensured United remain without an away win this season.

Lammens could have come to meet Iván Fresneda’s cross 100 times and probably dropped the ball only once. It was his and United’s misfortune that it should happen here. Suárez could barely believe his luck, although his finish was still accomplished, an acrobatic overhead kick from close range.

Senne Lammens with a gift for Luis Suárez to equalise for Sporting 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/kOQ6HImlVc.

Sources indicate that one of the stars of last season for United, Lammens is being dragged down with the rest of them this time around. He had looked hesitant from the moment he was almost caught dealing with a back-pass by Suárez in the opening minutes. It set the tone for what was to come.

As if Mauricio Pochettino did not already have enough on his plate, United’s latest head coach now has a goalkeeper problem.

Industry observers note that of course, this would not have been as costly a night for Lammens had Marciniak not made such a mess of things himself. United may have been their own worst enemies again, but there was little doubting Sporting were given a helping hand here by some truly wretched refereeing.

The worst of it was the denial of a perfectly legitimate equaliser late in the first half after Youri Tielemans was penalised for a perceived foul – it was nothing of the sort – that the referee had initially not blown for.

And then moments after Suarez made it 2-2, the Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira flapped at Fernandes’s corner and punched the ball into his own net. Kaique’s blunder was already in motion by the time Patrick Dorgu barged into Kaique. But Marciniak was ordered to the pitch-side monitor by Piotr Lasyk, the VAR, and from there, he weakly decided Kaique had been infringed upon by Dorgu. It was a major let-off for the goalkeeper and the hosts.

According to recent reports, to compounded United’s frustrations, they were then reduced to 10 men late on when Tielemans, who had been booked for protesting over the first disallowed goal, received a second yellow card. It means United have now had four red cards and conceded five penalties in their last five games and, four weeks shy of Christmas, are still searching for a win on the road.

Recent findings suggest that the irony was that, amidst the chaos, there was a lot Pochettino will have liked about the performance. It was far from perfect but United at least had a structure, coherence and confidence about them for long periods. But for Lammens’s shocker and some dubious refereeing, United would surely have claimed just a fourth win this season.

It has been revealed that the problem with this United side is they never seem too far away from an act of self-sabotage. Pochettino insisted on the eve of this game that his team were not fragile, but that assessment was challenged in the crazy 160 seconds when United conceded not one but two penalties.

Recent findings suggest that in truth, they could feel hard done to by the award of the first in the 29th minute. Geny Catamo went down far too easily – and very late – after Lisandro Martínez swung out a leg. There was contact but it was of the very minimal variety. Martínez rushed off to Marciniak to remonstrate but his pleas fell on deaf ears. There was a sense of justice, then, when Lammens saved Suárez’s feeble penalty.

You would have thought that would be a confidence booster for Lammens, but in no time he had gone from hero to zero, with worse to follow.

According to recent reports, A ball was swept in behind Noussair Mazraoui and Maximiliano Araújo gave chase. There was no need for Lammens to come careering out of goal but that is what he did. When he clumsily blocked off Araújo in the process, Marciniak wasted little time brandishing a yellow card and pointing to the spot. This time Suárez made no mistake from 12 yards.

What will please Pochettino is United did not crumble again from there. In fact, they rallied and would soon be nursing a sense of injustice for the second time in four days.

Already outraged by the circumstances around Leny Yoro’s rescinded red card against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, Pochettino now had to contend with some perverse refereeing from Marciniak.

In a recent development, tielemans had slipped a pass through to Amad Diallo, with his momentum carrying him into Gonçalo Inácio. Marciniak did not blow his whistle, presumably because in the moment he did not feel a foul had been committed. But after Diallo’s shot was saved and a split second before the Ivorian headed the rebound into the net, the Polish referee blew his whistle.

Tielemans could not believe what he was seeing and, to add insult to injury, was booked for his protestations.

The problem for United was that, because Marciniak had blown moments before Diallo put the ball into the net, VAR were powerless to review the decision.

After the match, Pochettino claimed United were punished by the referee’s decisions.

The Argentine was again in a state disbelief at some refereeing decisions, even though he appeared at pains not to land himself in hot water with Uefa.

In a recent development, “It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,” Pochettino said.

Recent findings suggest that on the foul awarded against Tielemans, he added: “I think everyone knows all that was… impossible [to understand]. You know, it’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field.”.

In a recent development, what Pochettino demanded was a strong start after the interval, and he got just that. A third penalty award of the night this time went United’s way. Martínez, who had been operating as an inverted left-back for much of the game, wriggled his way past Eduardo Quaresma before being bundled over from behind by the Sporting defender. Fernandes stepped up and coolly converted the penalty. This time it was Sporting’s turn to implode, even if Fernandes and United’s goal had some good fortune about it.

According to recent reports, fernandes was running to the right when he cut back inside, just outside the penalty area, and struck a speculative left-foot shot at Kaique. There appeared no obvious danger and then the ball seemed to hit a divot in the ground, seemingly created moments earlier by Fernandes as he slid in, and cannoned upwards. The Sporting goalkeeper was thrown by it and the next thing the ball was flying through his hands.

According to recent reports, united have had very little in the way of luck this season, so their supporters would argue it was long overdue. Misfortune, in the form of Lammens’s clanger and Marciniak’s refereeing, would soon come back to haunt them, though. What a job Pochettino has walked into.

With this type of situation [individual mistakes], always we need to do double effort. Concentrate, more. Focus, more. Performance is the best medicine to prepare the next game.

Sources indicate that [On Lammens] Mistakes are part of football, and from that comes goals. This is a team sport, and the notable thing is to stick together in good and bad moments. Everyone has to take the blame for everything we do good and we do bad as well.

Sources indicate that we need points to get through. We need to focus on the next one. Now the moment is to get back to the Premier League. We need to stick together and fight for our lives.

A much better United performance, undermined by a terrible night for their goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who conceded a penalty and dropped a simple cross when they had a second-half lead.

Before that, there were hints of a Pochettino team in United’s football: they were industrious, energetic and fully committed, and they were the better of two limited teams for long chunks.

Fernandes’ second goal, after scoring from the spot against his former team, will stick in the memory after the ball bounced off a divot and over the goalkeeper.

Although United were lucky there, they will feel referee Marciniak was against them, blowing up for a foul by Tielemans before Amad went through and judging that Sporting’s goalkeeper was fouled from a late corner.

One last Sporting break, but Irankunda skewed wide from a tight angle when he would have been better off crossing.

Breaking: Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on problems that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • Sources indicate that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on problems that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

Sources indicate that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

Sources indicate that "Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," states Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

Industry observers note that UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

Sources indicate that this economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Sources indicate that nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

Sources indicate that young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

In a recent development, he is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

In a recent development, "Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," indicates Brod.

Industry observers note that sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

According to recent reports, her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
  • "He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bellingham finished 11th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?

Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho noted.

"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world.".

Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.

While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.

"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10.".

While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?

BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.

Is Bellingham at the moment 'the best player in the world'?

Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.

He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.

It has been revealed that he leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.

He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.

When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.

He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.

While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.

But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.

The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".

He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.

Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.

Recent findings suggest that "It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level.".

Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.

He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.

Rice created 17 major chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.

In a recent development, the 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.

He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.

The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.

It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.

The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.

His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.

The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.

The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top.

Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.

The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.

He has created 26 chances from open play in La Liga this season, the sixth-highest total across Europe's top five leagues, and wins possession an average of 7.6 times per 90 minutes, the 10th-highest figure.

However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.

Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.

He might not yet have the profile of Barcelona team-mates Rodri or Pedri, but on current form alone, versatile youngster Lopez is one of Europe's best box-to-box goalscorers.

The 23-year-old already has nine goals and seven assists this season. Counting only goals scored in Europe's top five leagues and the Champions League, no central midfielder has more.

While Lopez can also operate on the wing, the presence of Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon means he has mainly featured as a number eight or a number 10 this term.

The Barcelona academy graduate played only a bit-part role as Spain won Euro 2024 and was unfortunate to miss the World Cup after breaking a bone in his foot in May.

However, a summer off enabled him to hit the ground running this season, and he has not looked back.

Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (459 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.
  • Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.
  • Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” stated marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson mentioned.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage highlighted the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and noted younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench highlighted a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson remarked.

The professor mentioned the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson stated, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he mentioned.

Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon.
  • In a recent development, to that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results.
  • "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon.

In a recent development, to that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal.

"We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement. "That's an key step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon.".

In a recent development, to grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith, the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions.

It has been revealed that the secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, stated in the same statement.

According to recent reports, the idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth.

NASA funding supported this research.

The biggest fear behind the Premier League’s controversial move to digital football tickets

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • Recent findings suggest that it is described as the Premier League’s “secret civil war”, except it’s very public.
  • This season’s full introduction of digital tickets has affected fan behaviour and community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Recent findings suggest that it is described as the Premier League’s “secret civil war”, except it’s very public. So much so that it affects the majority of those who fill stadiums every single week. It affects the lifeblood of football… but then the entire point is that this isn’t something tangible you can touch.

This season’s full introduction of digital tickets has affected fan behaviour and community.

Recent findings suggest that you can see it in queues outside games. You can hear it in discussions on the difficulty of “passing on” tickets, and arguably even atmosphere.

Duncan Drasdo of the Manchester United Supporters Trust says, “it absolutely impacts fan culture”.

The Football Supporters’ Association say they are “monitoring” how it progresses but it all plays into a deeper sense, that there is a long-term aim to eventually end season tickets altogether.

Multiple clubs contacted for this article strenuously dispute this, and many are quite strident on their position.

Recent findings suggest that the move comes from a vote in the summer of 2024, where there was effusive support for the mandatory introduction of digital tickets from the start of this season. This essentially means doing away with old physical tickets - although clubs can still give them out in special cases - for ones now scanned. And, if holders can’t go, they can pass to selected family and friends, or put on the club exchange.

According to recent reports, there are two primary arguments the clubs make. One is cutting down on touting, which they insist is still absolutely rife. Club sources say the data revealed networks where people were running 50-60 season-ticket accounts, and there was financial gain. They argue that runs contrary to the idea of the season ticket being personal to a fan for their loyalty, and insist the only action - achieved through hidden barcodes - is against abuse.

The other is increasing safety, and knowing everyone who is in the stadium. It inherently conditions better behaviour, since anyone can be tracked.

It has been revealed that fan groups accept parts of these arguments, and would acknowledge that a lot of their clubs directly engage, but sympathy has been eroded by direct experience. Almost immediately, there were long queues outside games, many of which have lingered. Most pertinently, though, there is the sudden negating of what has long been normal. Every season-ticket holder will know it, as will those who use their tickets. “Passing on” is a lot more difficult, as clubs increase obligation for the ticket to be used in some form.

In a recent development, “And passing it on is absolutely fan culture,” says Gareth Roberts, of Liverpool’s Spirit of Shankly group. Drasdo adds: “It’s what creates community.”.

A common complaint is that it now involves more laborious processes, and doing it unofficially potentially risks a ban, when you used to be able to just hand it to someone.

Recent findings suggest that “Not just talking about Liverpool here, but I do know of fans who do get worried about it,” Roberts claims. “There are so many rules and regulations to take in, it’s almost like taking an exam. It feels a heavy load to be a supporter.

According to recent reports, “Through not filling in the initial form as they wanted, I have one mate who can’t go to Champions League games and two who can’t go to cups. The assumption is that everyone is digitally literate, but they don’t.”.

This has practical concerns, too, if a fan can’t go at short notice.

In a recent development, “We’ve been saying there should be ways to do this,” Roberts states. “You’re not setting up a business and earning from this. OK, there are touts but they have to think of ways to not impinge on traditional fans.”.

It has been revealed that darren Epstein, a Gold Rep at Arsenal, says the complication of it all is under-appreciated: “In days gone by, we’d be talking about managers and tactics. Now it’s when away tickets go on sale, collections, ID checks, and points - points being the loyalty points you get on buying an away ticket.

It has been revealed that “It feels like a constant battle to ensure you get to a game. Although, changes have undoubtedly improved the ability of many fans to get to games they never have been able to before, which many of course feel is a good thing.”.

A connected complaint is that this is one more factor affecting traditional atmospheres.

According to recent reports, “If it’s the club re-selling the ticket on the exchange, it changes the profile of the support, introducing a random fan into a group of mates,” Drasdo claims. “In the old standing sections you were able to congregate with friends but the introduction of all-seater stadia meant people got split up by where their seats were and we lost that mobility which is the key to atmosphere.".

It has been revealed that tom Concannon of the FSA, speaking as a Newcastle United fan, claims: “Atmospheres are worsening because of it in my opinion. Tickets are going to those wanting to experience the atmosphere rather than contribute to it.” Roberts adds: “Atmosphere is dependent on youth vibrancy. The Kop is pretty old now.”.

Recent findings suggest that even in simple terms, it’s a lot harder to pass on tickets to children who may not have a phone, but that clubs actively need to get that match-day buzz. Fan representatives would similarly say it doesn’t help that the Premier League’s clubs’ ticketing working group only has heads of ticketing on it, rather than actual match-going fans.

It has been revealed that such concern feeds into a deeper tension in all of this, between being a supporter and being a customer. An irony is that it means fans have less control over what they pay for. As one executive indicates, “if you’ve bought your season ticket, you should have no obligation to sit in the seat”.

According to recent reports, another perspective is that clubs are being more strict and trying to get control of every ticket they can. One industry figure points to how the same data from digital tickets has allowed clubs to see just how often tickets are passed on, and it has stunned them. One club has estimated that 20-25 per cent of tickets are passed on, which they also see as running contrary to what a season ticket is supposed to be.

Or, as some fans put, they realised they could monetise. Tickets not passed on can be put on the ticket exchange, where FSA research shows prices are considerably higher than the average for a season-ticket seat.

Club sources would say they deliberately decoupled the season-ticket price from match-by-match, to recognise the value of a season-ticket holder.

Drasdo offers a different view: “A common phrase we hear from our fans is ‘the club are the biggest touts of all’, which is essentially a reaction to the restrictions on usage and the premium prices we see when season ticket holders' tickets are resold by the club.

“A major problem we’ve had at United is stretching the gap in price between season ticket holders and member ticket prices which causes the club to focus on how season ticket holders pass on their tickets when not personally attending.”.

Another knock-on has been what Roberts describes as the “normalisation” of fans who don’t have season tickets paying fees to become members to go into lotteries for tickets. Some clubs even charge for transferring. Most clubs have unlimited membership, meaning there is actually less chance of getting a ticket.

It has been revealed that “We’ll never really know how many tickets end up in the hands of actual fans,” Concannon claims. “Hospitality numbers are on the rise.”.

Clubs would nevertheless insist they are acutely conscious of this, and they have to allow opportunities for fans on long waiting lists, or who otherwise feel shut out of being able to go to games. That has fostered tension between supporters, as well as between supporters and clubs. Fans who speak out often find themselves shouted down by others who say “if you don’t pay it, I will”.

And yet such demand comes at a different cost, as anecdotal evidence suggests a lot of long-time supporters are being worn down. “There’s an underbelly of that growing, that clubs don’t realise,” Roberts argues. “If you’re constantly made to jump through these hoops.”.

According to recent reports, such weariness has even been deepened by two other concerns. One is this long-time fear that clubs actually want to get rid of season tickets, so they can sell more seats for higher prices. Club sources are adamant that is not the case, as illustrated by how season tickets stripped from some fans are redistributed to those on the waiting list. Whether that is true or not, a step like this could serve as a halfway step for the future.

In a recent development, clubs themselves would point to escalating player costs and fans wanting the best possible team on the pitch but, as with redundancies, this is dismissed. “A nonsense notion,” Concannon indicates, “£25 from every fan at every Premier League game only just paid the agents’ bills last season.”.

Industry observers note that one chief executive actually links the entire glitch to the financial rules. “The point of forcing bums on seats should be atmosphere,” they say. “The ugly extra money-making for clubs is not on. Clubs do need protection - if they had cost-control protection they would not be fleecing fans.”.

Sources indicate that some clubs would accept there could have been better communication. For now, if you go to a game this weekend, it’s what a lot of fans are talking about.

#139692. Industry News: West Ham are in danger of becoming the next Leicester

Industry News: West Ham are in danger of becoming the next Leicester

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.
  • It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer proposal and greater purpose.
  • Recent findings suggest that sometimes, though, relegation is just the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.

It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer proposal and greater purpose.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, though, relegation is just the start. If it is not taken seriously, relegation might not be rock-bottom, but a trapdoor that sends a club spiralling to upcoming lows.

Recent findings suggest that leicester City know all about that trapdoor. The Foxes were Premier League champions in 2016, FA Cup winners in 2021 and Conference League semi-finalists in 2021/22, but are now in League One after a series of relegations.

They were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware, but years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy saw them fall into the second tier and beyond.

West Ham United were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware - the Conference League in 2023 - but dropped out of the Premier League last season after years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sources indicate that the Hammers had been in the division since 2012 and finished as high as sixth in 2020/21, ending the campaign a place and a point behind Leicester. In 2024/25, the season before they went down, they generated the 20th-highest revenue in world football, according to the Deloitte Money League. Leicester were 17th in the Money League in 2021/22, the campaign before the first of their two recent relegations from the Premier League.

Both clubs boast facilities that are out of place in their division. West Ham’s 62,500-seater London Stadium has almost double the capacity of the next biggest Championship ground, while Leicester’s training complex is one of the best in the country, let alone League One.

Industry observers note that the parallels do not end there. Like Leicester 12 months ago, West Ham were one of the pre-season Championship promotion favourites and started the campaign well, but those results papered over the cracks.

Recent findings suggest that since climbing to second with a 1-0 victory at then-leaders Swansea City on October 17, the Hammers have gone six games without a win and sacked manager Nuno Espirito Santo, replacing him with Scott Parker. They are 13th ahead of today’s visit of second-place Stoke City, with 24 points from 17 matches.

It has been revealed that it is eerily similar to Leicester’s start to last season. Looking to make an immediate return to the Premier League, the Foxes were third on October 17. But like West Ham, results started to slide. Like West Ham, they had 24 points after 17 games.

Of course, Leicester’s season ended with relegation, and the Hammers are by no means destined for the drop. Right now, though, the parallels are impossible to ignore.

In terms of individual quality, both clubs began their respective seasons with one of the most talented squads in the league. Leicester had the likes of Abdul Fatawu, Jordan James and Stephy Mavididi, while West Ham can call on Jarrod Bowen, Konstantinos Mavropanos and Manor Solomon, among others.

Industry observers note that however, both squads bore the hallmarks of years of poor recruitment. Leicester’s group included several major-money signings that had failed to deliver, including Patson Daka, Oliver Skipp and Jannik Vestergaard, and they did not pay a single transfer fee in the summer 2025 window to try to balance the books.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, West Ham have a top-heavy squad filled with attacking quality but light on defensive cover. The Hammers spent almost £40million this summer - including paying an EFL-record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic - yet failed to address some glaring gaps in the squad.

In a recent development, with all those attackers, West Ham need a manager who wants to dominate games. But Nuno prefers to let the opponents have the ball and attack swiftly in transition, which was ill-suited to his squad. The Hammers have now appointed Parker, a Championship promotion specialist having previously taken Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley up.

It has been revealed that once again, it is strikingly similar to Leicester, who sacked Marti Cifuentes in January and turned to Gary Rowett, a Championship survival specialist. However, his pragmatic style did not get the best out of his players and the Foxes continued to slide.

This runs deeper than the managers, though. Any head coach at Leicester would have struggled to reinvigorate a group of players who had either lost belief or did not want to be at the club anymore.

In a recent development, that highlighted in their reaction to going behind. After November 8 last year, Leicester did not win a single Championship game in which they conceded first. If heads drop when you suffer a setback, it points to a lack of confidence, fight or both, and form will suffer.

This season, West Ham are yet to win in the league after going 1-0 down, drawing five times and suffering five defeats. They have conceded first in every game of their six-match winless run. This is the biggest red flag of the Hammers’ season so far. Having quality players means nothing if they do not have the right mentality, as Leicester found out last term.

According to recent reports, it remains very unlikely that West Ham follow the Foxes into League One. But their recent transfer business does not suggest they will recruit smartly in January and if they miss out on promotion, you would expect some of their better players to leave next summer - sparking a transition period and potentially an extended spell outside of the top flight.

Sources indicate that even if Parker turns it around and wins promotion, is he the right man to lead them in the Premier League? The Hammers manager is yet to succeed in a top-flight job and if he is sacked in 12 months time, you would not back the club’s hierarchy to identify the right replacement based on their track record.

That was another feature of Leicester’s decline. The Foxes won promotion at the first attempt in 2023/24 but made poor managerial choices in Steve Cooper and then Ruud van Nistelrooy, and were relegated immediately.

Five years ago, West Ham fans would have dreamed of being the ‘next Leicester City’. Right now, it is the nightmare scenario.

Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.

It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.

The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Bafode Diakite was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.

Bournemouth might have folded then, but instead they came roaring back, Alvaro Rodriguez heading them level almost immediately after the start of the second half.

According to recent reports, A draw would have been an excellent result in the circumstances. Substitute Rayan had other ideas, waiting at the end of a rapid breakaway to sweep in the winner 12 minutes from time.

Victory against Viktoria Plzen in December will almost certainly now be enough to earn direct passage to the last 16.

Pablo Duran had the ball in the Bournemouth net after 10 minutes after it spilled back to him off Michele Di Gregorio, the goalkeeper relieved to see the offside flag go up against the Celta striker.

In a recent development, the stand-in keeper redeemed himself minutes later with a solid save from an outrageous bicycle kick by Aspas. It would have been a remarkable goal but the Celta great would not be denied. Bournemouth failed fully to get the ball away, and from the edge of the box Aspas curled a beauty in off the far post.

According to recent reports, bournemouth had gone behind in the first half of their last game in this competition at Sparta Prague. That night, the balance was tipped almost immediately in their favour by a red card for the Czech side, but here it was Rose’s team who found themselves down to 10 men.

Diakite made an honest attempt to win the ball but was late and his studs landed on the ankle of Couhaib Driouech. An initial yellow card was overturned following a VAR check and Bournemouth were on the ropes.

It had been the most challenging half of their debut European campaign, but within minutes of the start of the second period, they were level.

Amine Adli was left in space outside the box to send over a wonderful cross to the far post. Arriving there was Rodriguez, sneaking ahead of his defender to get a head on the ball and nod in the equaliser.

In a recent development, A wonderful counter-attack brought the Premier League side their winner. Adrien Truffert showed good strength out on left to outmuscle Sergio Carreira, and he fed the ball up to Marcus Tavernier. He might have shot himself but instead moved it on to Rayan who swept home.

#139686. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (920 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most vital temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most vital temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

Sources indicate that the east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

Industry observers note that only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

Industry observers note that in 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

Industry observers note that the researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another vital discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

According to recent reports, using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most key fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Industry observers note that alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

According to recent reports, for years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

#139684. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1157 w)
